tool_input.body:
Closes `ethos-7tqd`, the last open bug in the cluster-2 triage (mission state persistence). The other four closed in #508.

## The bug

`ethos mission dispatch` writes the contract; a separate `Agent()` call spawns the worker. Something has to bridge that gap so the worker's delegation files under the right mission — that bridge was a session-wide binding that captured **the next spawn, whoever it was**.

Reproduced live 2026-09-07: a throwaway probe mission captured this leader's unrelated PR-fix agent as delegation `d-2026-09-07-039`. The audit trail is this project's product; a wrong delegation edge is silent data corruption, not a cosmetic issue.

The bead's original framing — "orphaned contracts sit inert, nobody notices" — was backwards and the triage note says so. They don't sit inert. They capture.

## What changed

**Bindings are per-mission, single-use, and scoped to the declared worker.** A pending dispatch lives in its own file keyed by mission ID. Only a spawn whose agent type matches the contract's `Worker` consumes it; a mismatched spawn proceeds unbound and leaves the binding for the real worker. `ethos mission claim` bindings are untouched and stay sticky by design.

**Delegations record how they were bound.** New `BoundVia` field over a closed set (`mission_id_env`, `inherited`, `active_mission_sidecar_claim`, `active_mission_sidecar_dispatch`). Records written before this change have an empty value, which is **never** treated as evidence a delegation may be disclaimed.

**`ethos mission abandon --disclaim <id>`** retires a mission whose only delegation was wrongly captured. Three mechanical gates — provenance must be exactly the dispatch value, verdict must not be open, not already disclaimed. No bypass flag; the result-artifact gate is untouched. Without this, a captured mission was permanently unretireable.

**Depth- and hash-refused delegations no longer block abandon.** Those skeletons are written before the worker runs, so they prove no work happened. Enforced by an AST guard over the write sites rather than a comment.

## Verification

- `make check` green including the race detector; `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...` exits 0.
- Detached test gate (harness env unset, outside Claude ancestry): 27 ok / 0 FAIL.
- Every behavioural change confirmed **failing** against pre-fix code before the fix landed, via `git stash` or targeted revert.

## Review history — why this branch is long

Three local reviewers over three rounds, plus the worker's own probes: **31 findings, 4 critical.** None would have been caught by CI. Highlights:

- **Two dispatches to the same worker handle destroyed the first binding**, so mission A's worker filed under mission B. This repo pins one handle per domain, so it was the normal path, not an edge case. Fixed by the per-mission redesign.
- **An unreadable contract permanently denied every spawn of that worker** — reachable by dispatching and then switching git branches, since contracts are tracked. Now skipped, never cleared (a failed read proves nothing).
- **Two concurrent spawns could claim the same binding.** This org's conventions call for batching independent tool calls, so concurrent spawns are normal here. Now locked.
- **A binding type inverted meaning**, and the code still carried the old cost analysis as its justification — so a corrupted file silently restored the original bug.

Four separate tests were found to guard their own fixture rather than their stated property — including, at one point, the drift guard added to prevent exactly that. All rewritten and falsified against mutated implementations.

`DES-076` records the decision and, deliberately, an explicit residual-risk section naming what this does **not** close. An earlier draft understated that, and three defects survived a full review round because readers trusted it.

## Follow-ups filed, not silently dropped

- `ethos-q5as` — audit vacuum reads sealed state from one checkout root (warn-only; cannot mask a real loss)
- `ethos-mzi6` — doc-comment misattachment in `cmd/ethos/session.go`
- `ethos-sg53` — a completed mission strands open when its worker's session ends before submitting a result

## Phase 3 verification

Driven through the real entry point throughout: this branch's own missions were dispatched and spawned using the code being changed, and the write-set conflict check shipped in #508 blocked creating a follow-up mission while a stale one was open — which is how `ethos-sg53` was found. Operator confirmation pending on this PR.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

tool_input.message:
The code reviewer re-read against `9ac02b6` and confirmed three of its six findings closed by J1/J2/J3 — verified, not assumed. It specifically checked the risk your J1 extraction could have introduced (`ethos mission dispatch` mutating another mission's pending entry as a side effect of composing an advisory string) and confirmed `ClassifyPendingDispatches` is pure, with the stale-clear correctly left inside the hook loop under the lock. Good call on where to draw that line.

Both high-risk lanes got a clean mechanical verdict: the classification switch is exhaustive, FIFO survives the extraction, per-session scoping holds, clear-before-remove ordering is right, and the retry-token semantics work — `Delete` correctly skips the lock-file removal when `deleteFiles` errors.

**PR #509 is open**, so these land as additional commits. Six items.

**A — the drift guard now detects correctly but still teaches the wrong criterion. Highest priority.** `aborted_writer_drift_test.go:16-18` still says the three sites "all fire BEFORE a worker process starts" — while its own `wantSites` at `:66` lists `store.go:Close`. That site stamps `aborted` on delegations at `verdict: open`, i.e. workers that ran. The test contradicts itself three lines apart, and `CHANGELOG.md:108-110` states it more strongly still ("written only by" the two refusals).

This matters beyond the wording: the guard exists to make the next maintainer re-justify a fourth writer, and "fires before the worker starts" would wave through a writer that stamps `aborted` on an *open* mission's delegation — the one thing that actually breaks the exclusion. The correct criterion already exists, well-written, at `store.go:1845-1856`: the Close sweep is unreachable from the gate because Abandon refuses unless the mission is `StatusOpen`. Lift it into the test and the CHANGELOG. The right rule is "no writer may stamp `aborted` on a delegation whose mission is still open."

**B — NEW, and it's a regression J3 introduced. `Purge()` swallows the error J3 just made consequential.** `internal/session/store.go:311,317`: `if s.deleteFiles(id) == nil { didPurge = true }`. On a sidecar-clear failure the session isn't purged, isn't in `purged`, has no `refused` slice to land in, and **nothing reaches stderr**. The operator sees a purge that silently did nothing.

That's strictly worse than pre-J3, which at least printed a line per failed sidecar. Both sibling callers get it right — `purgeOneTombstoned:544` logs and returns `didRefuse`; the unreadable-roster branch at `:361` logs. `Purge()` is the only swallowing one. Log it, and give `Purge` a `refused` return like its sibling.

**C — NEW. J5 left a dangling reference inside J3's doc comment.** `store.go:221` says the sidecar clear duplicates "internal/hook's `clearSessionMissionBindings`, which still runs FIRST and is now a harmless no-op double-clear." J5 deleted that function. Grep finds the name in exactly two places tree-wide: this comment and a stale one in `session_test.go:108`. Nothing runs first; there is no double-clear. Same class the branch has been chasing all week, introduced by the commit that removed the function, and sitting in the one comment a maintainer reads before touching `deleteFiles`.

**D — `Store.Abandon`'s own doc comments still state the pre-DES-076 gate.** `store.go:1252-1256` ("Any sign that work started… There is no override flag here either") and `:1335-1342` ("open, closed, any verdict… UNLESS an operator has explicitly disclaimed it", omitting the automatic aborted exclusion). K2/K5 fixed this exact sentence in `--help`, the MCP description, the deposited guide, and `docs/mission-abandon.md` — four surfaces — and skipped the function they describe. The authoritative comment now contradicts all four.

**E — my call, since the reviewer asked for a decision rather than guessing. Clear the sidecars on the refusal path.** `ethos session purge` → `PurgeTombstoned`, which returns before `deleteFiles` on an unreadable roster (`:355-359`) or `unsealed > 0 || probeFailed` (`:511-522`) without `--force`. A SIGKILL'd session is the canonical holder of unsealed lines, so the CHANGELOG's headline scenario is the one most likely to hit the refusal.

The reviewer's framing is right: **sidecars are not audit state.** The tombstone guard exists to protect unsealed audit lines; mission bindings are machine-local coordination state. Protecting the roster while clearing the bindings is coherent — the refusal preserves exactly what the guard is for, and clears what has no business surviving a dead session. Do that, which also makes the CHANGELOG claim true rather than needing to be softened.

Also add a `PurgeTombstoned` test: `TestStore_Purge_ClearsMissionSidecars` covers `Purge()`, which **no CLI command calls** — the only non-test caller is `PurgeTombstoned`. The CLI-reachable path has no sidecar test and none of its refusal branches are covered.

**F — low priority.** `*ast.ReturnStmt` still isn't a write position in the guard, so `func abortVerdict() string { return DelegationVerdictAborted }` is invisible and its callers register only as a `CallExpr` naming the helper. Needs an indirection to bite, but it's one line and the walk is already paid for.

**Minor, fold in only if you're touching either:** `ClassifyPendingEntry` (`active.go:691`) inlines `fmt.Sprintf("that mission is %s", ...)` while `nonOpenReason` (`pretooluse_dispatch.go:510`) produces the identical operator-facing string. Two copies in two packages, after a commit whose purpose was collapsing duplication.

Order: A, B, then C/D/E/F. On J6's second half — accepting the repeat-warning noise as a named residual rather than bolting on a cooldown marker with its own cleanup-coordination failure mode — I agree with the call, and recording it in DESIGN.md instead of claiming a fix you didn't make is exactly right.
